content: In at least 5% of isolates, a threshold is reached that necessitates changes in treatment guidelines. Additionally, three countries in the region have reported at least a 5% decrease in susceptibility in recent years. Only two countries, New Caledonia and the Philippines, reported no isolates with decreased susceptibility in any reporting year. In the Region of the Americas, Canada and the USA reported decreased susceptibility to ceftriaxone, with Canada reporting rates exceeding 5%. Both countries also reported decreased susceptibility to cefixime in less than 5% of isolates. Data on ceftriaxone susceptibility is more limited in other regions. In the South-East Asia Region, only two countries reported ceftriaxone susceptibility data for 2012/2013. Of the seven countries reporting to GASP between 2009 and 2013, five reported some decreased susceptibility to ceftriaxone, with four of these countries reporting rates exceeding 5%. In the African Region, only one country, Côte d’Ivoire, reported decreased susceptibility to ceftriaxone, with rates exceeding 10%, while South Africa reported less than 5%. In the Eastern Mediterranean Region, no countries reported decreased susceptibility to ceftriaxone in 2012/2013. Since 2009, only four countries in the African Region and two in the Eastern Mediterranean Region have submitted data, with only Côte d’Ivoire and South Africa reporting decreased susceptibility to ceftriaxone. The first documented treatment failure with ceftriaxone occurred in Japan, followed by additional failures in Austria, Australia, Canada, France, Norway, Slovenia, South Africa, Sweden, and the United Kingdom. Regarding azithromycin, among 42 countries reporting susceptibility data in 2012/2013, 17 reported resistance in 5% or more of isolates. Only seven countries reported no resistant isolates. Most countries reporting during this period were in the European Region, where 13 of 24 countries reported resistance in 5% or more of isolates, and nine countries reported rates exceeding 10%. Cyprus and Greece reported resistance rates exceeding 20%. Three countries in the European Region reported no resistant isolates, although two of these had reported resistance in previous years, and the third submitted antimicrobial resistance (AMR) data for the first time in 2013. Countries in Asia began reporting azithromycin susceptibility data in 2011. Of the four countries reporting from the South-East Asia Region between 2011 and 2013, three reported resistance in less than 5% of isolates, and one reported no resistance. In the Western Pacific Region, six of nine reporting countries identified resistant isolates, with Japan reporting rates exceeding 10% in both 2012 and 2013. In the Region of the Americas, all four reporting countries, including Canada and the USA, identified resistant isolates, with Chile reporting resistance rates exceeding 5%. No countries in the Eastern Mediterranean Region submitted data. Côte d’Ivoire was the first country in the African Region to report AMR for azithromycin in 2013, with resistance rates exceeding 10%. For quinolones, 56 countries reported ciprofloxacin susceptibility data in 2012/2013. High levels of resistance were observed across all regions, with nearly every country reporting resistance rates exceeding 20%. Twelve countries, mostly in Asia, reported extremely high resistance levels, with over 90% of isolates resistant. Only four countries—Dominican Republic, Fiji, New Caledonia, and Panama—reported resistance rates below 5%, although the Dominican Republic had previously reported rates exceeding 20%. The WHO guidelines for treating gonococcal neonatal ophthalmia recommend ceftriaxone (50 mg/kg intramuscularly, up to a maximum of 150 mg) as a single dose. Alternatives include kanamycin (25 mg/kg intramuscularly, up to a maximum of 75 mg) or spectinomycin (25 mg/kg intramuscularly, up to a maximum of 75 mg). These recommendations are based on very low-quality evidence but emphasize the importance of treatment due to the significant benefits. Treatment choice may depend on cost, drug quality, and equity considerations. Side effects should be monitored in neonates.
